title: Vibration Analysis Services vs. Continuous Monitoring: What Routes Leave Unwatched
summary: Vibration analysis services check assets monthly or quarterly. Learn what failures between routes cost and which assets need continuous monitoring.
body_markdown:
## Key Points


- [Vibration analysis](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/vibration-analysis) **services and periodic routes capture a snapshot.** They show asset condition on the day of the reading, not the days in between.
- **Most breakdowns happen in the gap.** We analyzed 60,898 real-world breakdowns across several North American plants. 48% happened 2-30 days after the asset’s last closed inspection, and 57% hit before the next scheduled visit.
- **The gap drives**[reactive maintenance](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/reactive-maintenance) **.** Failures between visits mean[unplanned downtime](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/unplanned-downtime) , emergency labor, collateral damage and rushed parts.
- **Remote**[condition monitoring](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/condition-monitoring) **closes the gap on**[critical assets](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/critical-assets) **.** Continuous sensors detect changes as they develop, so teams act before a fault becomes a failure.
- **The best programs are hybrid.** Use continuous monitoring on high-consequence, fast-changing or hard-to-reach assets. Keep routes for broad screening of lower-risk equipment.


## Are vibration analysis services enough to cover critical assets?


No, not on their own. Vibration analysis services and periodic routes are effective for screening, but they only see an asset when someone takes a reading. For critical assets with fast-changing failure modes, limited access or high downtime cost, a monthly or quarterly snapshot leaves most of the operating time unwatched.


The issue isn't the quality of the analysis. A skilled analyst can read a spectrum accurately and still miss a fault that develops two weeks after the route. Coverage depends on timing, access, route completion, analyst capacity and how fast the team acts on the report. When any one of those slips, the asset runs without visibility.


## How do vibration analysis services and condition monitoring services work?


Most route-based programs follow the same cycle:


1. A technician, in-house or from a condition monitoring services provider, walks a set list of assets on a fixed schedule, usually monthly or quarterly.
2. The technician collects vibration readings with a handheld data collector.
3. An analyst reviews the data, often days or weeks later.
4. The plant receives a report with findings and recommended actions.
5. The maintenance team creates work orders and schedules the repairs.


This model works well for:


- **Broad screening** across hundreds of assets at a low cost per point
- **Human inspection context** that a sensor can't provide, such as sounds, smells, leaks and visual damage
- **Low-to-medium consequence assets** where a slower failure or a spare on the shelf limits the risk


The limitation is built into the model. Each step adds delay, and the asset is only measured once per cycle.


## What do periodic vibration routes miss?


Periodic routes miss failures that develop between visits, and that is where most breakdowns happen. Tractian analyzed 60,898 breakdowns from a full year of maintenance data across North American plants. Every one occurred on an asset that had a closed inspection or PM work order before it failed.


Time from last closed inspection to breakdown Share of breakdowns


Same or next day 7%


2 to 7 days 16%


8 to 30 days 33%


More than 30 days 45%


**48% of breakdowns occurred 2 to 30 days after the last inspection.** 57% occurred before the next scheduled visit was due.


These assets were inspected and cleared. Then conditions changed:


- **Lubrication degraded** faster than the PM interval assumed.
- **Components loosened** under load, including base bolts, couplings and fixings.
- **Operating conditions shifted.** A new product, speed or load introduced a failure mode the last reading never captured.
- **Fast-developing faults progressed** from detectable to functional failure in days.


A route cannot detect what happens after the technician leaves. That is the limit of any snapshot-based program.


## What does the gap between routes cost?


The gap between routes turns planned maintenance into reactive maintenance. When an asset fails between visits, the cost goes well beyond the repair:


- **Unplanned downtime.** Production stops on the asset's schedule, not yours.
- **Emergency labor.** Overtime, call-ins and contractor premiums.
- **Collateral damage.** A dry bearing becomes a scored shaft. A minor repair becomes a rebuild.
- **Expedited parts.** Rush freight, or waiting on a spare that isn't in stock.
- **Safety exposure.** Work done under time pressure carries more risk.


The hidden cost is capacity. Every surprise failure pulls technicians off planned work. Backlog grows, PMs slip and the next failure becomes more likely. For understaffed teams, that cycle is hard to break.


Outsourcing the route does not solve it. The snapshot moves to a vendor’s schedule, and the report still arrives after the reading. Even when the warning does come, acting on it is its own challenge.[According to Verdantix](https://tractian.com/en/verdantix-study-report) , 80% of plants say they have difficulty turning alerts into proactive actions. A finding that sits in a report or an inbox is still a gap.


## Example: how one sawmill caught failures between scheduled checks


A North American sawmill uses continuous monitoring on the equipment that keeps logs moving through the mill.


Sensors on the bark hog detected a change in bearing condition between scheduled checks. The team inspected, found the bearings under-lubricated and greased them. The asset stayed in service, and the team avoided an estimated 8 hours of downtime from that single catch.


Over the following weeks, the same system flagged three more developing faults:


Asset Fault found Action


Canter head Knives broken by tramp metal Knives replaced


Band mill motor Cooling fans clogged Fans cleaned, back in service


Debarker motor Loose base bolts Tightened between shifts


***Together, the four catches added up to six figures in reported savings.***


These were common faults: lubrication, contamination and looseness. Each one was caught while it was still a minor task, not a teardown.


## Vibration analysis services vs. remote condition monitoring


**Remote condition monitoring** , also called online condition monitoring or remote vibration monitoring, uses permanently installed sensors to measure asset condition continuously. Instead of a reading once a month, the team sees changes as they develop and gets alerted when a fault starts to form.


Vibration analysis services (routes) Remote condition monitoring


Data frequency Monthly or quarterly snapshot Continuous


Time to detection Next route plus analysis time As the fault develops


Coverage between visits None Full


Hard-to-reach or hazardous assets Often skipped Monitored remotely


Readings under real load Depends on timing Captured during operation


Best fit Broad screening, lower-risk assets Critical, fast-changing or hard-to-reach assets


Continuous monitoring only pays off when alerts are accurate and lead to action. Look for a system that diagnoses the fault, ranks it by priority and connects it to a work order, so detection turns into a completed repair.


## How to decide which assets need continuous monitoring


Not every asset needs a sensor. Every critical risk needs a coverage plan. Use these five steps to build one:


1. **Rank assets by consequence.** Score production impact, safety risk, repair cost and whether a spare or redundant unit exists.
2. **Estimate failure speed.** Identify assets whose common failure modes can progress from detectable to failed in less than one route interval.
3. **Check access.** Flag assets that are hazardous, guarded, elevated or hard to measure under normal load.
4. **Review your breakdown history.** Find assets that failed within 30 days of a clean inspection. Those are your proven gaps.
5. **Assign a strategy to each asset.** Continuous monitoring for high-consequence, fast or inaccessible assets. Routes or handheld checks for the rest. Run-to-failure only as a deliberate choice.


## Frequently asked questions


### **What are vibration analysis services?**


Vibration analysis services are outsourced programs where a provider collects vibration data from plant equipment on a set schedule, analyzes it and reports on asset condition. Most use handheld collectors on monthly or quarterly routes.


### **What is the difference between condition monitoring services and remote condition monitoring?**


[Condition monitoring](https://tractian.com/en/glossary/condition-monitoring) services usually rely on periodic, manual data collection. Remote condition monitoring uses installed sensors that send data continuously, so changes are detected between visits instead of at the next route.


### **How often should vibration routes be run?**


Most plants run routes monthly or quarterly. The right interval depends on how fast an asset's failure modes develop. If a fault can progress to failure faster than the route interval, the asset needs continuous monitoring.


### **Can remote vibration monitoring replace routes entirely?**


Not usually. Most plants get the best results from a hybrid program: continuous monitoring on critical assets, and routes for broad screening and inspection of lower-risk equipment.


### **How does continuous monitoring reduce reactive maintenance?**


It detects developing faults such as lubrication loss, looseness and misalignment early enough to schedule the repair. That turns an unplanned breakdown into planned work.


## What is that gap costing you?


Periodic vibration analysis is a valid part of a reliability program. But a snapshot only covers the day it was taken, and the data shows most breakdowns happen after it.


Before your next service contract renewal, pull last year's breakdowns and answer one question: **what is the gap between routes costing us?** Count the failures on assets that passed their last inspection. Add the downtime, overtime, rushed parts and lost production. That total is the cost of what your routes leave unwatched.
